artboards.title: B2 · The map — lines, stops and interchanges
B · A node as the learner reads it
C · Entering from a Labs decision

annotations.text:
B2 — a transit map. Click the three-position control.

This is MetroSets, a published hypergraph visualisation method: hyperedges drawn as coloured lines running through their member nodes on a schematic map. It is the answer to both problems at once. A track is a LINE; a node is a STOP; a node several tracks depend on is an INTERCHANGE — so the reusable-node claim becomes something you can see rather than a paragraph. And it is drawn like an instrument, not a game: octilinear segments, hairlines, one colour, no glow.

Zones across the top are the regions. Level 0 shows your line; level 1 brings up the tracks that share your stops; level 2 adds the minor stops nobody names.

Settled spends no colour — Labs' own law, which the previous constellation version broke.

A — the highest-risk screen in the project.

Measured finding: teacher-revised AI items carry MORE flaws than teacher-only ones. Automation bias, visible as low interaction density.

So Approve is inert with its three unmet conditions listed above it: mark every unsourced assertion, then answer the node's own checks. The claim is already locked — it gates everything else.

B — one node, all its holes rendered.

Green band = the per-track FRAMING hole, the escape from the reusability paradox. Red band = the misconception. Then two different things: a CHECK (90 seconds, comes back on a spacing schedule) and a PROBLEM (the actual gate — solving it is what marks the node solid).

B3 — Rosalind's shape, which is the thing that made Rosalind last 14 years: statement, Given/Return, sample dataset, sample output, YOUR dataset, one auto-graded answer.

Two additions. A rung ladder, because a wet-lab biologist did not sign up to program and rung 1 must be solvable in a text editor. And the wrong-answer nudge is generated from the node's own recorded misconception — not from a model reading your answer.

C — the forcing function no competitor has.

Left is Mendel's tier-3 decision with its rule, premise and citation. Right is Code, entered FROM it.

The drawer leads with what you need to judge the decision yourself. The short answer is present but last, and framed as the rule's reasoning — that is the cognitive-surrender guard the MIT report argues for.
